analysis.one_liner: Sets minimum nurse-to-patient ratios in every U.S. hospital, with protections for nurses who refuse unsafe assignments.
analysis.headline: A bill to set federal nurse-to-patient ratios in hospitals drew 99 Democratic cosponsors but died in committee without a hearing or vote over two years.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require every hospital in the country to staff its units with no more than a set number of patients per nurse — for example, one nurse for every four patients in a medical-surgical unit. Hospitals would have to post their actual staffing levels publicly, keep records for three years, and could be fined up to $25,000 for a first violation. Nurses who believe an assignment is unsafe or understaffed could refuse it without being fired, and Medicare payments to hospitals would be adjusted to cover the added cost of compliance.
analysis.who_benefits: Hospital patients, who get a guaranteed minimum number of nurses on every unit and shift; registered nurses and licensed practical nurses, who get enforceable workload limits, required breaks, protection from mandatory overtime, and legal protection if they refuse an assignment that would endanger patients; and rural communities, which get extra time (four years instead of two) to meet the ratios.

how_it_helps.text: The bill sets unit-by-unit maximum patient loads per registered nurse: one patient in trauma and operating rooms, two in intensive care and burn units, three in emergency rooms and pediatrics, four in medical-surgical units, and up to six in well-baby and postpartum units [S3].

Hospitals must post actual nurse-to-patient ratios in each unit where patients and staff can see them, keep three years of records open to the public, and undergo federal audits; hospitals that violate the rules can be fined up to $25,000 for a first violation and $50,000 after that, and their names published by HHS [S3].

Nurses may refuse an assignment that violates the ratios or that they are not trained to perform safely, and hospitals may not fire, discipline, or report them to licensing boards for it; nurses who are retaliated against can sue for reinstatement, back pay, and attorney's fees [S3].

The bill bans using mandatory overtime to meet staffing requirements, bans counting video monitors or administrators toward the ratio, and prohibits averaging ratios across shifts to hide short-staffing [S3].
Medicare payments to hospitals would be increased to cover the net additional cost of meeting the ratios, based on a MedPAC cost study, so the mandate would not simply be an unfunded one [S3].
The bill adds stipends to the nurse scholarship program and expands nurse retention grants to include preceptorship and mentorship projects, aimed at easing the nursing shortage [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals, which would have to hire substantially more registered nurses, comply with posting and record-keeping rules, and face federal fines and public naming for violations; and federal taxpayers, who fund the Medicare payment adjustments that cover hospitals' added compliance costs.

drawbacks.text: The country has a real nursing shortage; a hard ratio requirement can only be met with nurses who must exist. The bill addresses this through recruitment stipends, retention grants, and a congressional report on the nurse supply, but critics could reasonably argue the mandate may outpace the workforce, and the bill does not force states to produce more nurses [S3].

Even with Medicare payment adjustments, the added cost of hiring thousands of nurses would ultimately be borne largely by taxpayers and by hospitals with thin margins, including some rural hospitals already struggling financially; the bill mitigates this by giving rural hospitals four years instead of two to comply [S3].

Fixed numeric ratios are a one-size-fits-all tool: patient needs vary within a unit and across hospitals, which is why the bill requires additional staffing above the minimum based on patient acuity — but that judgment layer adds complexity and enforcement burden [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — patients not lying understaffed and nurses not running themselves into the ground — is backed by the studies Congress itself cites in the bill's findings, including research on California's ratio law showing improved patient outcomes at no additional cost. The real costs are labor: hospitals must hire, and Medicare must pay. The serious practical risk is the nursing shortage; a mandate without enough nurses could strain rural hospitals in particular, which the bill's longer rural timeline partially addresses. On balance this is a well-developed bill whose main cost is money, aimed squarely at patient safety.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees in April 2023 and then to a health subcommittee, and over nearly two years no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 6, 2023 by Rep. Jan Schakowsky and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee [S5].
It gathered 98 cosponsors, all Democrats, alongside its Democratic sponsor — 99 members total [S4].
On April 14, 2023 it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, and on December 17, 2024 it was referred to that subcommittee again [S5].
No further action — no hearing, no subcommittee or committee vote, no floor vote — appears anywhere in the bill's action history before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals, which avoided a federal mandate to hire more nurses, post their staffing publicly, and pay federal fines; patients and nurses did not get the ratios or the refusal protections.

sides.party_line_note: All 99 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, with no Republican support recorded, and the bill died in committee in a chamber controlled by Republicans.

industries.note: Hospitals would have had to hire many more registered nurses, post actual staffing levels publicly, keep three years of records, and face fines up to $50,000 per violation — a direct hit to the labor savings that come from running units short-handed. Medicare would have offset compliance costs, but the mandate, audits, and public naming would remain.

industries.industry: Registered nurses and licensed practical nurses
industries.note: Bedside nurses would gain enforceable workload caps, guaranteed competence-based assignments, required rest and meal breaks, a ban on mandatory overtime, and the legal right to refuse unsafe assignments without retaliation.

industries.industry: Temporary and travel nurse staffing agencies
industries.note: The bill requires agency nurses to prove unit competence and get orientation before assignment, and adequate permanent staffing would reduce hospitals' reliance on costly agency labor. Agencies that benefit from chronic understaffing would face less demand; agencies providing competent, oriented staff would not be shut out.
